passage:
Dear Baljeet paaji,
You asked in your last message whether I've started my chemistry project on polymers. Technically, no. But I have a plan. I work way better under pressure, you know that. Remember my Class 9 model? Built the night before, and it got an A. So there's no point starting now when the deadline is ten days away.
Also, I've been watching videos about polymers, which counts as research. Tonight I'll watch just one more and then open the file.
Honestly, when I open the project sheet, it's full of words like "monomer" and "condensation", and my head goes a bit blank. It's easier to close it and do it later, when I'm in the mood.
Anyway, how's college in Patiala? Is the canteen food as bad as you said?
Your cousin,
Lokesh

qa.q: What happened with Lokesh's Class 9 model?
qa.a: It was built the night before, and it got an A.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's head going 'a bit blank' suggest about the real reason for the delay?
qa.a: It suggests the delay is about avoiding the uncomfortable feeling of not understanding words like 'monomer', not about having plenty of time.

qa.q: What could Lokesh try instead of 'one more video' tonight?
qa.a: Lokesh could open the sheet and look up just one confusing word, or ask Baljeet paaji to explain 'monomer', so the blank feeling shrinks.

qa.q: How might Baljeet paaji read this letter?
qa.a: Baljeet may smile at the 'pressure' excuse but notice the line about the blank head and guess that Lokesh feels nervous about the topic.

grounding: Shows a teenager giving reasonable-sounding excuses for delaying a project while the real reason is avoiding the uncomfortable feeling of not understanding it.

passage:
Charu, trust me, your friend Rekha has it sorted. The history essay's due Monday, it's Friday, that's like three whole days. I always do better at the last minute anyway; my brain just switches on.
Right now I'm only watching one video, then I'll start. Okay, maybe this one too, it's only twelve minutes. It's basically a break before the real work, which is supposed to be good for you, right?
Why are you looking at me like that?
Fine. The truth is, last time Mrs Dsouza wrote "shallow analysis" in red across the top, and every time I open the document I see those words. So yes, I'd rather watch someone fold paper cranes. At least nobody writes in red on paper cranes.
Okay, don't laugh. You're laughing.
One more video. Then the essay. Probably.

qa.q: What did Mrs Dsouza write across Rekha's last essay?
qa.a: "Shallow analysis", in red across the top.

qa.q: Why would Rekha rather watch videos than open the essay?
qa.a: Every time the document opens, Rekha sees 'shallow analysis' in red, so the videos are a way to avoid that sting of being judged.

qa.q: What could Charu suggest to help Rekha start?
qa.a: Charu could suggest writing just one messy first sentence together, or asking Mrs Dsouza what deeper analysis looks like, so the red words feel less scary.

qa.q: What might Charu be thinking while Rekha explains the videos?
qa.a: Charu's look suggests doubt about the 'last minute' excuse, and Charu may sense that something else is holding Rekha back 🤔.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager claiming to work better at the last minute and starting 'after one video', while the delay is really about avoiding the sting of past criticism.

passage:
Lokesh, beta, you say you work better under pressure? Ha. I said the same thing when I was fifteen. Let me tell you.
Every evening I had a reason. "I'll start after the cricket score." "My mind is fresh only after dinner." "I'm a pressure player, like a batsman in the last over." My mother believed me. I believed me.
But the truth, beta? I was scared of the maths. Every time I opened the book I felt stupid, and the excuses made that feeling go away for a while. It was never about time.
The night before the exam, I sat up till three, panicking. I scraped through. Your old Shankar Dada knows: the excuse is usually hiding a feeling.

qa.q: What did Shankar say he would start after?
qa.a: The cricket score.

qa.q: What feeling was young Shankar really avoiding?
qa.a: Young Shankar felt scared and stupid on opening the maths book, and the excuses made that feeling go away for a while.

qa.q: In the story, what could Shankar have done instead of making excuses?
qa.a: Admitted being scared of maths and asked for help, or started with a small part of it early.

qa.q: How might Shankar's mother have felt if she'd known the truth?
qa.a: She might have been surprised and concerned, wanting to help him with the fear rather than trusting the excuses.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling teenage excuses about working better under pressure, which were really avoiding the feeling of being bad at maths.

passage:
The house was full of cousins for the wedding next week, and Uday's physics test was on Monday. "I can't study with all this noise," he told his sister Kavitha. "Anyway, I work best under pressure. I'll start Sunday."
"You said that last time."
"And I passed, didn't I?"
He picked up his phone. "One video. Then I'll start."
One video became four. Kavitha watched him scroll, then asked quietly, "Uday, what's actually hard about the physics?"
He stopped. "Electricity. I don't get it. When I open the chapter I feel dumb."
"So it's not the noise."
Uday put the phone face down. "...Maybe not."

qa.q: When was Uday's physics test?
qa.a: On Monday.

qa.q: What feeling was Uday really avoiding with his excuses?
qa.a: He was avoiding feeling dumb and confused about electricity, not a lack of time or quiet.

qa.q: What turning point did Kavitha's question create?
qa.a: It helped Uday see the real feeling behind the delay, so he could ask for help with electricity.

qa.q: How might Kavitha feel watching him scroll?
qa.a: Kavitha seems patient but concerned, sensing the excuses were hiding something.

grounding: Shows a teen using noise and working under pressure as excuses, which turn out to be about avoiding feeling dumb.

passage:
Lalit sat at his desk in their Kolkata flat with the history essay open. Blank. "I'll start after one video," he told himself. "Just to relax my brain." It sounded sensible.
At nine, Urmila di peeked in. He was on his fourth video. "Essay?"
"I work better at night. Fewer distractions."
At eleven, he told himself he'd do it fresh in the morning. At midnight he was reorganising his pens.
Lying in bed, he admitted it to the ceiling. Every time he looked at the essay question, his stomach dropped. What if he wrote something stupid? The videos weren't about relaxing. They were about not feeling that drop.

qa.q: What subject was Lalit's essay for?
qa.a: History.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling each time he looked at the essay question?
qa.a: He felt a drop of fear and self-doubt, worried he would write something stupid.

qa.q: What small step could Lalit try tomorrow?
qa.a: Naming the fear and writing just one rough sentence before any video.

qa.q: What might Urmila di be thinking when she peeks in?
qa.a: Urmila di may be amused but a bit worried, seeing that the essay still hasn't started.

grounding: Shows a teen whose reasonable-sounding excuses cover the real reason for delay: avoiding the fear of writing something stupid.

passage:
"Deepak, the history project is due Friday." Kunal leaned on the doorframe, eating an apple.
"I know. I work better under pressure, bhaiya. You know that."
"It's Tuesday."
"Exactly. Plenty of time." Deepak scrolled on. "I'll start after this one video. It's about the Mughals, so it's basically research."
"It's a cooking video."
"It's a Mughlai cooking video."
Kunal laughed. "What's the project actually on?"
"Trade routes. Twelve pages." Deepak's thumb stopped. "I opened the file on Sunday. It just sat there blank, and I got this horrible heavy feeling. Homework-flavoured dread."
"So it's not really about time, is it?"
Deepak put the phone face down. "Maybe it's about the blank page."
"Then don't fill a page. Write the title and one heading. I'll sit here with my apple."

qa.q: How many pages is the trade routes project?
qa.a: Twelve pages.

qa.q: What feeling is Deepak really avoiding?
qa.a: A heavy dread at the blank page, which he covers with excuses about working better under pressure.

qa.q: What small step does Kunal suggest, and why could it help?
qa.a: Writing just the title and one heading, which makes starting feel lighter than facing twelve blank pages.

qa.q: How does Kunal see Deepak's excuses?
qa.a: He finds them funny but sees through them, gently pointing out that the problem is not really about time.

grounding: Shows a teen excusing delay with working better under pressure and one more video, while the real reason is avoiding an unpleasant feeling.
